Choosing an assembly method

Source: vignettes/Assembly-Methods.Rmd
Assembly-Methods.Rmd

RiboPilot can build the ribosomal repeat from your reads in three ways. GetOrganelle is the default. The other two use SPAdes and are there for samples GetOrganelle cannot assemble: baited assembles only the reads that match the reference database, and de-novo assembles every read.

The method is chosen per sample, under Assembler in the Assembly Options window of the Assemble step. Everything after assembly (quality checks, annotation, export) works the same whichever you pick.

If you already have an assembly for a sample, you can skip assembly altogether. See Already have an assembly?.

At a glance

GetOrganelle (default) SPAdes, baited SPAdes, de-novo
How it works Recruits ribosomal reads with the seed database, then extends and assembles them over several rounds Maps reads to the seed database, then assembles only the pairs that match Assembles all reads, then keeps the contigs that match the label database
Uses the reference database for Recruiting reads and picking ribosomal contigs Recruiting reads and picking ribosomal contigs Picking ribosomal contigs only
Speed and memory Moderate Fastest, lowest memory Slowest, highest memory
Best for Most samples Samples where GetOrganelle fails or returns only short contigs Samples where both of the others fail, or a cross-check on a doubtful result
Watch out for Can fail to extend when coverage is low or uneven Only recovers what resembles the reference, so contigs can stop short in the variable spacer regions Runtime and memory; more contigs to review

How long each one takes

One sample from the test project, run three times on the same desktop with each assembler, gives a sense of scale. The sample (SRR14163830, a pufferfish) has 1.4 million read pairs of 2 x 150 bp. Each run had 6 CPUs and up to 24 GB of memory. The times and memory are for the assembly step alone; the rest of the workflow (read cleanup, quality checks, annotation) added about two minutes in every case.

GetOrganelle SPAdes, baited SPAdes, de-novo
Assembly time 1 min 20 s 19 s 38 min 30 s
Peak memory 2.9 GB 0.3 GB 4.1 GB
Contigs 1 (8,960 bp) 3 (5,031, 2,223, and 564 bp) 11 (longest 6,159 bp)

GetOrganelle gave the whole repeat in one piece. Baited SPAdes was the fastest by far, but split the same repeat into three contigs. De-novo SPAdes took about thirty times longer than GetOrganelle, and about a hundred times longer than baited, and left more fragments to review. Larger read sets scale these numbers up, and de-novo scales up the most.

Where to start. Use GetOrganelle for the whole project. Switch a sample to baited SPAdes when it fails. Keep de-novo SPAdes for the few samples that neither of the others can assemble.

GetOrganelle

GetOrganelle starts from a seed database of known ribosomal sequences, recruits the reads that match, and extends outward from them round after round. A label database then picks out which parts of the result are ribosomal. Both databases come from the Reference step, so a database built for the right group matters more here than any option.

The GetOrganelle options box carries its command-line flags. The GetOrganelle wiki explains them.

SPAdes, baited

Baited assembly is the first thing to try on a sample that failed. Reads are mapped to the seed database with Bowtie 2, only the read pairs that match are kept, and SPAdes assembles that small pool. Contigs that match the label database are kept; the rest are discarded.

Because the read pool is small, this is quick and light on memory. The cost is that a read must resemble the reference to be kept. The genes (18S, 5.8S, 28S) are conserved and recruit well. The spacers between them vary much more, so on a sample distant from everything in the database a contig can end early or break at a spacer.

Two boxes control it:

  • bowtie2 options. How reads are matched to the seed database. The default is --local.
  • SPAdes options. The default is --isolate. If SPAdes rejects the reads with these flags, the run is retried once with no extra flags.

SPAdes, de-novo

De-novo assembly skips the baiting step and gives SPAdes every read. The reference database is used only afterwards, to keep the contigs that match the label database. Nothing is filtered up front, so this can recover a repeat whose reads the seed database fails to recruit.

It is also by far the most expensive method, since it assembles all of the sequencing reads. Raise Memory (GB) in the Assembly Options window if a sample fails for lack of memory. Only the SPAdes options box applies.

Mixing methods in one project

Since assembly options are saved as named sets, a project can use GetOrganelle for most samples and SPAdes for the difficult ones. Open a sample’s Assembly Options cell, type a new Parameter set name, tick Edit, choose the assembler, and press Save. The Assemble walkthrough shows this on a failed test sample.

A GenBank submission records one assembly method. If an export group mixes assemblers, the Export step offers to split it.
